item.title: Thirty-Two Connections and an Empty File: A Race in Turso's Page-1 Allocation
item.description: ePHPm runs PHP inside a Rust server. For SQLite-style databases it uses Turso, a rewrite of SQLite in Rust that is still labeled beta. I recently hammered ePHPm’s per-site mode with brand-new sites. A burst of first requests to a new site could panic inside the engine. This post is about where that panic came from and how to fix it. How Turso got into ePHPm is in Clustered SQLite, Part 2.

item.title: os/exec's StdoutPipe Footgun: How cmd.Wait() Ate My Last Frame (Twice)
item.description: shipmates spends most of its life spawning claude (and codex) processes and reading newline-delimited JSON off their stdout. The last frame of a turn is the important one. It’s a result frame with the cost, the model and the final text. Stderr matters too, because that’s where Claude Code tells you Invalid API key · Please run /login. For a while I was throwing both away under load. The cause is documented right there in the os/exec godoc. I fixed it in one package and then found the exact same bug again a month later in another.

item.title: Stop Running PHP on tokio's spawn_blocking - Own Your Thread Pool
item.description: For most of its life, ePHPm ran every PHP request on tokio’s spawn_blocking pool. It works. It passes tests and it serves benchmarks fine. It’s the first thing anybody reaches for when they need to call blocking code from async Rust. It’s also quietly wrong for a language runtime. The problems only show up under overload or after a crash. Over the last three weeks it got replaced with a pool of OS threads that ePHPm owns. That pool shipped first behind a config flag, then as the default. As of v0.9.0 the spawn_blocking engine is gone.

item.title: Two Small go-proxmox Fixes: A Watch Channel That Never Closed, and WithRetry
item.description:
